263: \section{Four-fermion operators and contact interactions}\label{contact}
264: 
265: The SM parity-violating (chiral) gauge symmetries and spontaneous/explicit breaking of these symmetries for the $W$ and $Z$ gauge boson 
266: masses and the hierarchy pattern of fermion masses have been at the 
267: centre of conceptual elaboration for possible scenarios beyond. The No-Go theorem \cite{Nielsen:1981xu, 1981PhLB..105..219N} shows that as a renormalizable quantum field theory at infrared (IR) low energies, the SM {\it bilinear} fermion Lagrangian at ultraviolet (UV) cutoff $\Lambda_{\rm cut}$ suffers theoretical inconsistencies with SM chiral gauge symmetries and fermion spectra at low energies. 
268: It implies that the BSM Lagrangian at $\Lambda_{\rm cut}$ should have {\it quadrilinear} operators \cite{Xue:2016dpl, Xue2017}
269: \begin{eqnarray}
270: \sum_{f=1,2,3}G_{\rm cut}\, \Big[\bar\psi^{f}_{_L}\psi^{f}_{_R}\bar\psi^{f}_{_R} \psi^{f}_{_L}\Big]_{q=0,-1,2/3,-1/3},\quad G_{\rm cut}\propto \Lambda^{-2}_{\rm cut},
271: \label{q1}
272: \end{eqnarray}
273: which is SM gauge symmetric four-fermion interactions of left- and right-handed fermions ($\psi^f_L,\psi^f_R$) in the SM charge sector ``$q$'' and flavour family ``$f$''. They are four-fermion operators of Nambu-Jona-Lasinio (NJL) or Einstein-Cartan type. Their origins at the scale $\Lambda_{\rm cut}$ are due to unknown grand unified interaction or quantum gravity dynamics.  
274: 
275: The strong four-fermion coupling $g_{\rm cut }\propto G_{\rm cut}\Lambda^2_{\rm cut}$ dynamics leads to composite bosons $\Pi^{f}\sim (\bar\psi^{f}_{_R} \psi^{f}_{_L})$ and fermions $F^{f}_R\sim \psi^{f}_{_R} (\bar\psi^{f}_{_R} \psi^{f}_{_L})\sim \psi^{f}_{_R}\Pi^{f}$ \cite{Xue1996, Xue2000, Xue2000a}. They 
276: are represented by the
277: mass (pole) and form factor (residue) of propagators, behaving as elementary particles after form-factor renormalisation. These composite particles carry SM quantum numbers and couple to massless SM gauge bosons. Their massive spectra preserve SM gauge symmetries, and constituents can 
278: be leptons, quarks or leptoquarks. There exists a UV fixed point $g^*_{\rm cut}$ and scaling domain, which realises an SM gauge symmetric, renormalizable {\it bilinear and dimensional-4} Lagrangian of composite bosons and fermions at the composite scale $\Lambda\ll \Lambda_{\rm cut}$ \cite{Xue2014, Xue2017}. 
279: As the energy scale decreases below $\Lambda$, the effective theory undergoes \cite{Xue2023} a phase transition of composite particles decay into constituents and spontaneous SM symmetries breaking via the top-quark channel $(\bar t_Lt_R\bar t_R t_L)$, realising the $\bar tt$-composite Higgs boson  
280: at the electroweak scale $v\approx 246$ GeV \cite{Bardeen1990}. The scale $\Lambda\approx 5.1$ TeV is estimated by using the top quark and Higgs boson masses and extrapolating the renormalization-group solution to the high-energy regime \cite{Xue2013}.
281: 
282: In this section we describe the four-fermion operators and contact interactions that are relevant for the study of the phenomenology of the composite bosons at $pp$ or $ep$  collisions, 
283: including the LHC, which will be detailed in Sec.~\ref{PhenomenologyCompositeFermions}.
284: 
285: We consider, among four-fermion operators (\ref{q1}) in introduction, the following SM gauge-symmetric and fermion-number conserving four-fermion operators, 
286: \begin{eqnarray}
287: &&G\left[(\bar\ell^{i}_Le_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})
288: +(\bar\ell^{i}_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})\right] + {\rm h.c.},
289: \label{bhlql}
290: \end{eqnarray}
291: and
292: \begin{eqnarray}
293: &&G\left[(\bar\ell^{i}_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}\ell_{Li})
294: +(\bar\ell^{i}_Le_{R})(\bar e_{R}\ell_{Li})\right]+ {\rm h.c.}\nonumber\\
295: &&G\left[(\bar\ell^{i}_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\ell_{Li})
296: +(\bar\ell^{i}_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\ell_{Li})\right]+ {\rm h.c.}
297: \label{bhlql1}
298: \end{eqnarray}
299: and
300: \begin{eqnarray}
301: &&G\left[(\bar\psi_{Lia}\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}\psi_{Lia})
302: +(\bar\psi_{Lia}e_{R})(\bar e_{R}\psi_{Lia})\right] + {\rm h.c.},
303: \label{bhlql2}\\
304: &&G\left[(\bar\psi^{bi}_Lu_{Rb})(\bar u^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})+(\bar\psi^{bi}_Ld_{Rb})(\bar d^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})\right] + {\rm h.c.},
305: \label{qbhlql}
306: \end{eqnarray}
307: being the SM doublet $\ell^i_L=(\nu^e_L,e_L)$ and singlet $e_{R}$ with an additional right-handed neutrino $\nu^e_{R}$ for leptons;
308: $\psi_{Lia}=(u_{La},d_{La})$ and $u^a_{R}, d^a_{R}$ for quarks, 
309: where the color $a,b$ and $SU_L(2)$-isospin $i$ indexes are summed over.
310: Eqs. (\ref{bhlql})-(\ref{qbhlql}) 
311: are for the first family only, as a representative of the three fermion families.
312: The SM left- and right-handed fermions are mass eigenstates, their masses are negligible 
313: in TeV-energy regime and small mixing among three families encoded 
314: in $G$ is also neglected \cite{xue2016_2}.
315: 
316: From Eqs. (\ref{bhlql}), (\ref{bhlql1}) and (\ref{bhlql2}), we give explicitly quark-lepton interactions of three types,
317: \begin{eqnarray}
318: &&G\left[(\bar e_Le_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}d_{La})
319: +(\bar\nu^{e}_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}u_{La})+ (\bar\nu^{e}_Le_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}u_{La})\right] + {\rm h.c.},
320: \label{bhlqlex}\\
321: &&G\left[(\bar\nu^e_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\nu^e_{L})+
322: (\bar e_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}e_{L})
323: +(\bar\nu^e_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\nu^e_{L})+
324: (\bar e_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}e_{L})\right] + {\rm h.c.},\nonumber\\
325: &&G\left[(\bar u^a_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}u^a_{L})
326: +(\bar d^a_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}d^a_{L})+ (\bar u^a_L e_{R})(\bar e_{R}u^a_{L})
327: +(\bar d^a_L e_{R})(\bar e_{R}d^a_{L})\right] + {\rm h.c.},\nonumber
328: \end{eqnarray}
329: for the first generation. $\nu^e,e,u,d \rightarrow \nu^\mu,\mu,c,s$ for the second generation, and $\nu^e,e,u,d \rightarrow \nu^\tau,\tau,t,b$ for the third generation.

482: \subsection{Contact interaction of composite bosons, quarks and leptons}\label{spqq}
483: 
484: As shown in Fig.~\ref{compositeBv}, 
485: the effective coupling between composite boson 
486: and its two constituents can be written as an effective contact interaction, 
487: \begin{eqnarray}
488: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^\pm}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}}(\bar d^a_{R}u_{La})\Pi^- + {\rm h.c.},\label{ciqlB}\\
489: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^0_d}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}} (\bar d^a_{R} d_{La})\Pi^0_d + {\rm h.c.},
490: \label{iqlBd}\\
491: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^0_u}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}}(\bar u^a_{R} u_{La})\Pi^0_u + {\rm h.c.},
492: \label{iqlBu}
493: \end{eqnarray}
494: and 
495: \begin{eqnarray}
496: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^{+5/3}_a}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}}(\bar e_{R}u_{La})\Pi^{+5/3}_a + {\rm h.c.},\label{ciqlBql}\\
497: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^{-1/3}_a}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}}(\bar\nu^e_{R}d_{La})\Pi^{-1/3}_a + {\rm h.c.},\label{ciqlBql1}\\
498: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^{2/3}_{u_a}}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}} (\bar \nu^e_{R}u_{La}) \Pi^{2/3}_{u_a} + {\rm h.c.},
499: \label{iqlBuql}\\
500: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^{2/3}_{d_a}}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}}(\bar e_{R} d_{La})\Pi^{2/3}_{d_a} + {\rm h.c.},
501: \label{iqlBdql}
502: \end{eqnarray}
503: where $g_{_{\rm Y}}=(F_\Pi/\Lambda)^2$.
504: Appropriate normalizing the composite boson $\Pi$ with the 
505: form factor $(g^*/F_\Pi)^2$ in Eqs. (\ref{nB0}-\ref{uB0}),  
506: the effective contact interaction in Eqs. (\ref{ciqlB}-\ref{iqlBu}) and (\ref{ciqlBql}-\ref{iqlBdql}) can be expressed as a dimensionless Yukawa coupling $g_{_{\rm Y}}$, 
507: whose value, corresponding to $F_\Pi$ value, 
508: can be different for composite bosons in Eqs.~(\ref{nB0}-\ref{uB0}) and (\ref{nB5/3}-\ref{uB2/3}), but we do not consider such difference here.
509: These are relevant contact interactions for phenomenological studies of possible inelastic channels of composite-fermion production and decay in  $pp$ or $ep$ collisions.
510: 
511: \red{We discuss the issue of generation mixing for four different charged types of LQ states: $\Pi^{5/3}_{a}$, $\Pi^{-1/3}_{a}$  $\Pi^{2/3}_{u_a}$ and $\Pi^{2/3}_{d_a}$ in Table \ref{qnuP0ql}. Each type has three copies due to generations, taking as example $\Pi^{5/3}_{a}\sim (\bar e_{R}u_{La})$, $\Pi^{5/3}_{a}\sim (\bar \mu_{R}c_{La})$ and $\Pi^{5/3}_{a}\sim (\bar \tau_{R}t_{La})$. If the LQ $\Pi^{5/3}_{a}$ is produced by, then decay to its constituents in the same generation, the Yukawa coupling $g_Y\sim {\mathcal O}(1)$ as given in Eqs.(\ref{ciqlBql}-\ref{iqlBdql}). Now we consider $\Pi^{5/3}_{a}$ is produced by $e$ and $u$ of the first family, and the branching ratio of decaying to $\tau$ and $t$ of the third family. The Yukawa coupling $g_Y\sim {\mathcal O}(1)$ for $e$ and $u$ production, and another Yukawa coupling $g'_Y$ for decaying to $\tau$ and $t$. The Yukawa coupling $g'_Y$ is a new parameter and $g'_Y < g_Y$, possibly $g'_Y\ll g_Y$ for the following reasons. The left- and right-handed fields of leptons and quarks, which make composite bosons and fermions, are the SM gauge eigenstates in each generation. They are the same as the mass eigenstates without considering generation mixing. If we need to consider the mixing, see the unitary flavour transformations eqs (15,16) for quarks and eqs (23, 24) for leptons in my article JHEP 2016 ref. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1605.01266.pdf. Using these unitary transformations $U^{\nu,\ell, u,d}_{L,R}$, we can rewrite the Yukawa couplings (\ref{ciqlB})-(\ref{iqlBdql}) by associating two unitary matrices $(U)^\dagger U$ which are unknown. As example,  by interacting (\ref{ciqlBql}) the $e$ and $u$ produced $\Pi_a^{5/3}$ will decay to $\tau$ and $t$ by interacting
512: \begin{eqnarray}
513: {\mathcal L}^{\rm \Pi^{+5/3}_a}_{\rm CI} &=& g_{_{\rm Y}}(U^\dagger_R U_L) (\bar \tau_{R}t_{La})\Pi^{+5/3}_a + {\rm h.c.} = g'_{_{\rm Y}} (\bar \tau_{R}t_{La})\Pi^{+5/3}_a + {\rm h.c.} ,\label{ciqlBqlmix}
514: \end{eqnarray}
515: where $g'_{_{\rm Y}} = g_{_{\rm Y}}(U^\dagger_R U_L)$, 
516: and the notation $(U^\dagger_R U_L)$ stands for relevant unitary transformations between generations considered. The general mixing matrix $(U^\dagger_R U_L)$ of leptoquark sector, see eq (35) of my JHEP 2016, has its analogies CKM matrix in quark sector, PMNS matrix in lepton sector. In conclusion, the general mixing matrix $(U^\dagger_R U_L)$ is totally unknown, the effective way for dealing with composite states of different generations but the same SM quantum numbers is to introduce a new Yukawa coupling. These discussions also apply to the three nonLQ composite bosons $\Pi^-$, $\Pi^0_u$ and $\Pi^0_d$ see eqs. (\ref{ciqlB})-(\ref{iqlBd}). It can be considered as a general rule for considering the initial and final states are not in the same family.}

711: \subsection{The type 2 of $G\left[(\bar\ell^{i}_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\ell_{Li})
712: +(\bar\ell^{i}_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\ell_{Li})\right]+ {\rm h.c.}$ (\ref{bhlql1}) }

714: In Eqs.~(\ref{bhlql1}), each four-fermion operator has the two possibilities to form composite fermions, listed in Tables \ref{nuF0+} and \ref{qnuF0+}.
715: Up to a form factor, $D$ ($U$) indicate a composite fermion composed by a down quark $d$ (an up quark $u$) and a color lepton quark pair $\Pi_a$, and its superscript for electric charge.
716: In Eq.~(\ref{bhlql1}), there are four independent composite fields $F$: 
717: $U^0_R$, $U_R^-$, $D_R^0$, $D^-_R$ and their Hermitian conjugates:
718: $\bar U^0_L=(U^0_R)^\dagger\gamma_0$, $\bar U^+_L=(U^-_R)^\dagger\gamma_0$, $\bar D^0_L=(D^0_R)^\dagger\gamma_0$,$\bar D^+_L=(D^-_R)^\dagger\gamma_0$, .

808: \section{contact interaction of composite fermions}
809: 
810: The contact interactions for the production and decay of a 
811: composite fermions $F$ are:
812: \begin{eqnarray}
813: {\mathcal L}^{F}_{\rm CI} = {\mathcal V}_{F} +{\mathcal V}_{F}^\dagger. 
814: \label{cieF}
815: \end{eqnarray}
816: In the case of Eq.~(\ref{bhlql1}) and Table \ref{nuF0+},
817: \begin{eqnarray}
818: {\mathcal V}_{\bar U^0} &=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar U^0_{L} u^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\nu^e_{L}), \quad pp~\rightarrow \bar U^0_{L} \nu^e_{L};\quad p\nu_L~\rightarrow \bar U^0_{L} u^a_{R},
819: \label{cieFf0+}\\ 
820: {\mathcal V}_{\bar U^+}&=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar U^+_{L}u^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}e_{L}), \quad pp~\rightarrow \bar U^+_{L}e_{L};\quad ep~\rightarrow \bar U^+_{L}u^a_{R},
821: \label{cinuFf0+}\\
822: {\mathcal V}_{\bar D^+} &=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar D^+_{L}d^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}e_{L}),
823: \quad pp~\rightarrow \bar D^+_{L}e_{L}; \quad ep~\rightarrow \bar D^+_{L}d^a_{R},
824: \label{cieF0+}\\
825: {\mathcal V}_{\bar D^0} &=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar D^0_{L}d^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\nu^e_{L}), \quad pp\rightarrow \bar D^0_{L}\nu^e_{R};\quad p\nu_L\rightarrow \bar D^0_{L}d^a_{R},
826: \label{cinuF0+}
827: \end{eqnarray}
828: and their Hermitian conjugates,
829: \begin{eqnarray}
830: {\mathcal V}^\dagger_{U^0} &=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar u^a_{L} U^0_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}u_{La}),\quad U^0_{R}\rightarrow \bar  u^a_{L}(\bar\nu^e_{R} u_{aL}),
831: \label{dcieFf0+}\\
832: {\mathcal V}^\dagger_{U^-}&=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}
833: (\bar u^a_{L}U^-_{R})(\bar e_{R}u^a_{L}),\quad U^-_R\rightarrow\bar u^a_{L}(\bar e_{R}u_{aL}),
834: \label{dcinuFf0+}\\
835: {\mathcal V}^\dagger_{D^-} &=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar d^a_{L}D^-_{R})(\bar e_{R}d^a_{L}),\quad D^-_{R}\rightarrow \bar d^a_L(\bar e_{R}d_{La}),
836: \label{dcieF0+}\\
837: {\mathcal V}^\dagger_{D^0} &=& \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar d^a_{L}D^0_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}d^a_{L}),\quad D^0_{R}\rightarrow \bar d^a_{L}(\bar\nu^e_{R}d_{La}).
838: \label{dcinuF0+}
839: \end{eqnarray}
840: In the case of Eq.~(\ref{bhlql2}) and Table \ref{QF0+},
841: \begin{eqnarray}
842: &&{\mathcal V}_{\bar E^{-2/3}_{Lb}} = \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar E^{-2/3}_{Lb} e_{R})(\bar e_{R}u_{Lb}); \!\!\!\quad\!\!\! ee~\rightarrow \bar E^{-2/3}_{La} u_{Rb};\!\!\!\quad\!\!\! ep~\rightarrow \bar E^{-2/3}_{La} e_{R};
843: \label{cieQf0+}\\ 
844: &&{\mathcal V}_{\bar N^{1/3}_{Lb}}= \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar N^{1/3}_{Lb}\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}d_{Lb}); \quad \bar\nu_R\nu_R~\rightarrow \bar N^{1/3}_{La}d_{Ra}; \quad p\nu_R~\rightarrow \bar N^{1/3}_{La}\nu^e_{R},
845: \label{cinuQf0+}\\
846: &&{\mathcal V}_{\bar E^{1/3}_{Lb}} = \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar E^{1/3}_{Lb}e_{R})(\bar e_{R}d_{Lb});
847: \quad ee~\rightarrow \bar E^{1/3}_{Lb}d_{Lb};
848: \quad ep~\rightarrow \bar E^{1/3}_{Lb}e_{R},
849: \label{cieQ0+}\\
850: &&{\mathcal V}_{\bar N^{-2/3}_{Lb}} = \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar N^{-2/3}_{Lb}\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}u_{Lb}); \!\!\!\quad\!\!\!
851: \bar\nu_R\nu_R~\rightarrow \bar N^{-2/3}_{Lb}u_{Rb}; \!\!\!\quad\!\!\!
852: \bar\nu_Rp~\rightarrow \bar N^{-2/3}_{Lb}\nu^e_{R},
853: \label{cinuQ0+}
854: \end{eqnarray}
855: and their Hermitian conjugates,
856: \begin{eqnarray}
857: \!\!&&{\mathcal V}^\dagger_{E^{2/3}_{Rb}} \!=\! \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar e_LE^{2/3}_{Rb})(\bar u^b_{R} e_{L}); \!\!\quad\!\!
858: E^{2/3}_{Rb}\rightarrow \bar  e_{L}(\bar u^b_{R} e_{L}),
859: \label{dcieQf0+}\\
860: \!\!\!&&{\mathcal V}^\dagger_{N^{-1/3}_{Rb}}\! = \!\frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}
861: (\bar\nu^e_{L}N^{-1/3}_{Rb})(\bar d^b_{R}\nu^e_{L});\!\!\!\quad\!\!\! N^{-1/3}_{Rb}\!\!\rightarrow\!\bar\nu^e_{L}(\bar d^b_{R}\nu^e_{L}),
862: \label{dcinuQf0+}\\
863: \!\!\!&&{\mathcal V}^\dagger_{E^{-1/3}_{Rb}}\! = \!\frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar e_{L}E^{-1/3}_{Rb})(\bar d^b_{R}e_{L});
864: \!\!\!\quad\!\!\! E^{-1/3}_{Rb}\!\!\rightarrow\! \bar e_{L}(\bar d^b_{R}e_{L}),
865: \label{dcieQ0+}\\
866: \!\!&&{\mathcal V}^\dagger_{N^{2/3}_{Rb}} \!=\! \frac{g_*^2}{\Lambda^2}(\bar\nu^e_{L}N^{2/3}_{Rb})(\bar u^b_{R}\nu^e_{L});\!\!\quad\!\!
867: N^{2/3}_{Rb}\rightarrow \bar\nu^e_{L}(\bar u^b_{R}\nu^e_{L}).
868: \label{dcinuQ0+}
869: \end{eqnarray}
870: These are relevant contact interactions for phenomenological studies of possible inelastic channels of composite-fermion production and decay in  $pp$ or $ep$ collisions.

873: \subsection{Contact interaction of $\Pi^{0,\pm}$ composite boson and gauge bosons}\label{spgg}
874: 
875: However, we shall consider other decay channels at the next leading order, such as neutral composite boson decay to two SM gauge bosons $\Pi^0_{u,d}\rightarrow \tilde G + \tilde G'$. We need a figure for $\Pi \rightarrow \tilde G + \tilde G'$. 
876: Note that the discussions here in this section do not apply to LQ composite bosons $\Pi^Q_a$ at this leading order, because that SM gauge bosons are zero or integer electric charges and the fractionally charged LQ composite bosons cannot decay to SM gauge bosons. \red{
877: The composite bosons $\Pi^{0,\pm}$ have two components: the pesudo scalar and scalar component. As example $\Pi^+=(g^*/F_\Pi)^2(\bar d^a_{R}u_{La})$ (\ref{nB0}) and $\Pi^0_u=(g^*/F_\Pi)^2(\bar u^a_{R}u_{La})$ (\ref{uB0}) are \cite{xue2017} 
878: \begin{eqnarray}
879: \Pi^+ &=&(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\bar d^a\frac{(1-\gamma_5)}{2}u_{a}= (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar d^au_{a}-\bar d^a\gamma_5u_{a}\Big)\label{twocomp+}\\
880: \Pi^0_u &=&(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\bar u^a\frac{(1-\gamma_5)}{2}u_{a}= (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar u^au_{a}-\bar u^a\gamma_5u_{a}\Big),
881: \label{twocomp0u}\\
882: \Pi^0_d &=&(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\bar d^a\frac{(1-\gamma_5)}{2}d_{a}= (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar d^ad_{a}-\bar d^a\gamma_5d_{a}\Big),
883: \label{twocomp0d}
884: \end{eqnarray}
885: which can be generalized to the 2nd and 3rd generations. In the following studies of composite bosons decaying to two SM gauge bosons via a fermion loop,
886: for the sake of notations, we use the $\Pi^{0,\pm}$ also for the pseudoscalar component with $\gamma_5$ presence, and introduce Higg-like ${\rm H}^{0,\pm}$ for  scalar component without $\gamma_5$ presence. Namely, henceforth, for pseudoscalar composite bosons
887: \begin{eqnarray}
888: \Pi^+ &=& (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar d^a\gamma_5u_{a}\Big)\label{twocomp+}\\
889: \Pi^0_u &=& (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar u^a\gamma_5u_{a}\Big),
890: \label{twocomp0u}\\
891: \Pi^0_d &=& (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar d^a\gamma_5d_{a}\Big),
892: \label{twocomp0d}
893: \end{eqnarray}
894: and for scalar Higg-like ${\rm H}^{0,\pm}$ bosons
895: \begin{eqnarray}
896: {\rm H}^+ &=& (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar d^au_{a}\Big)\label{htwocomp+}\\
897: {\rm H}^0_u &=& (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar u^au_{a}\Big),
898: \label{htwocomp0u}\\
899: {\rm H}^0_d &=& (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar d^ad_{a}\Big).
900: \label{htwocomp0d}
901: \end{eqnarray}
902: These can be generalized to the 2nd and 3rd families, ${\rm H}^0_t = (1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\Big(\bar t^at_{a}\Big)$ can be the candidate of the second Higgs particle, a massive and tightly bound state.}
903: 
904: Analogously to $\pi^0\rightarrow \gamma\gamma$, the massive $\Pi^0_{u,d}$ composite boson (pesudo scalar component) can also decay into two gauge bosons \cite{xue2017} :
905: \begin{eqnarray}
906: \Pi^0_{u,d} &\rightarrow& \gamma +\gamma, \label{cpg}\\
907: \Pi^0_{u,d} &\rightarrow& \gamma +Z^0,\label{cpgz} \\
908: \Pi^0_{u,d} &\rightarrow& Z^0 + Z^0, \label{cpzz} \\
909: \Pi^0_{u,d} &\rightarrow& W^+ + W^-,\label{cpww}
910: \end{eqnarray}
911: via the contact interaction
912: \begin{eqnarray}
913: {\mathcal L}^{\Pi^0}_{\tilde G\tilde G'} = \sum_{i=u,d}\frac{ gg^\prime N_c}{4\pi^2
914: F_\Pi}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}(\partial^\rho A^\mu)(\partial^\sigma A^{\prime\nu})\Pi^0_i,
915: \label{PiGG} 
916: \end{eqnarray}
917: where $g$ and $g^\prime$ represent the 
918: couplings of gauge bosons $A^\mu$ and $A^{\prime\nu}$ to the SM quarks $u$ 
919: and $d$ with different $SU_L(2)$-isospin $i=u,d$. 
920: Actually, this effective contact 
921: interaction (\ref{PiGG})
922: is an axial anomaly vertex, as a result of a triangle quark loop and standard renormalization procedure in SM. The color factor $N_c=3$ comes from the trace over color space of quarks in loop. The contact interaction (\ref{PiGG}) can be written as 
923: \begin{eqnarray}
924: {\mathcal L}^{\Pi^0}_{\tilde G\tilde G'} = \sum_{i=u,d}\frac{ gg^\prime N_c}{4\pi^2
925: F_\Pi}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\frac{1}{4}(F^{\rho\mu})(F^{\prime\sigma\nu})\Pi^0_i.
926: \label{PiGG1} 
927: \end{eqnarray}
928: \red{These amplitudes or effective interacting Lagrangians are the same, independent of quark types and masses in triangle loop. Therefore, it is the same and generalized for all generations. In addition, $\Pi^0_{u,d}$ decay to two gluons
929: \begin{eqnarray}
930: \Pi^0_{u,d} &\rightarrow& \tilde g
931: + \tilde g,\label{cpgg}
932: \end{eqnarray}
933: via the contact interaction
934: \begin{eqnarray}
935: {\mathcal L}^{\Pi^0}_{\tilde g\tilde g'} &=& \sum_{i=u,d}\frac{ g_s^2/2}{4\pi^2
936: F_\Pi}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}(\partial^\rho A^\mu_a)(\partial^\sigma A^{\prime\nu}_a)\Pi^0_i\nonumber\\
937: &=& \sum_{i=u,d}\frac{ g_s^2/2}{4\pi^2
938: F_\Pi}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\frac{1}{4}(G^{\rho\mu}_a)(G^{\prime\sigma\nu}_a)\Pi^0_i,
939: \label{PiGGg} 
940: \end{eqnarray}
941: where the strong coupling $g_s$ and $\alpha_s=g_s^2/(4\pi)$, the trace over color space gives $\tr(T^aT^b)=\delta^{ab}/2$, leading to $(G^{\rho\mu}_a)(G^{\prime\sigma\nu}_a)$ summed over color index $a$, see Ref.~\cite{anomalyS}.

Thus their triangle diagram contributions to the anomaly, i.e., $\pi^0$ decays to two gluons, are the same, but opposite in sign, therefore exactly canceled each other. In our case, $\Pi^0_u$ and $\Pi^0_d$ are different states, and both decay to two gluons and amplitudes are the same.}

35: def unbalanced(text: str) -> Optional[str]:
36:     """Why ``text`` has unbalanced brackets, or None when it is balanced.
37: 
38:     Mathematica strings ("...") and comments ((* ... *), nested) are skipped. An
39:     unbalanced verbatim string renders into a .fr that FeynRules stops reading
40:     with "Unexpected end of file" or "Invalid syntax", long after the schema
41:     said OK.
42:     """
43:     stack: List[Tuple[str, int]] = []
44:     i, n, depth = 0, len(text), 0
45:     while i < n:
46:         c = text[i]
47:         if depth:                                  # inside a comment
48:             if text.startswith("(*", i):
49:                 depth, i = depth + 1, i + 2
50:             elif text.startswith("*)", i):
51:                 depth, i = depth - 1, i + 2
52:             else:
53:                 i += 1
54:             continue
55:         if text.startswith("(*", i):
56:             depth, i = 1, i + 2
57:             continue
58:         if c == '"':                               # string literal
59:             i += 1
60:             while i < n and text[i] != '"':
61:                 i += 2 if text[i] == "\\" else 1
62:             if i >= n:
63:                 return "unterminated string literal"
64:             i += 1
65:             continue
66:         if c in _OPEN:
67:             stack.append((c, i))
68:         elif c in _CLOSE:
69:             if not stack or stack[-1][0] != _CLOSE[c]:
70:                 ctx = text[max(0, i - 30):i + 1]
71:                 return f"unexpected '{c}' at character {i} (...{ctx})"
72:             stack.pop()
73:         i += 1
74:     if depth:
75:         return "unterminated comment"
76:     if stack:
77:         c, j = stack[-1]
78:         ctx = text[j:j + 30]
79:         return f"'{c}' at character {j} is never closed ({ctx}...)"
80:     return None

392:     """Names of other parameters referenced by ``p``'s value/rules/definitions."""

404: def topo_sort_parameters(params: List[Parameter]) -> List[Parameter]:
405:     """Order parameters so each is defined before others that reference it.
406: 
407:     Stable (preserves input order among independent params). Raises on a
408:     dependency cycle.
409:     """
410:     names = {p.name for p in params}
411:     deps = {p.name: _param_refs(p, names) for p in params}
412:     by_name = {p.name: p for p in params}
413: 
414:     ordered: List[Parameter] = []
415:     emitted: set = set()
416:     remaining = [p.name for p in params]  # preserve input order
417: 
418:     while remaining:
419:         progressed = False
420:         still: List[str] = []
421:         for n in remaining:
422:             if deps[n] <= emitted:
423:                 ordered.append(by_name[n])
424:                 emitted.add(n)
425:                 progressed = True
426:             else:
427:                 still.append(n)
428:         remaining = still
429:         if not progressed:
430:             raise ValueError(
431:                 f"cyclic parameter dependency among: {sorted(remaining)}"
432:             )
433:     return ordered

439: def _block_entries(p: Parameter, sizes: Dict[str, int]) -> set:
440:     """The LHA entries (index tuples) an External parameter occupies in its block."""

445:         m = re.fullmatch(rf"\s*{re.escape(p.name)}\s*\[([0-9,\s]+)\]\s*", r.lhs)
446:         if m:
447:             entries.add(tuple(int(x) for x in m.group(1).split(",")))
448:     if entries:
449:         return entries
450:     ranges = [range(1, sizes.get(i, 3) + 1) for i in p.indices]
451:     out = {()}
452:     for rg in ranges:
453:         out = {e + (k,) for e in out for k in rg}
454:     return out

461:     scalar under (block, OrderBlock). Two parameters on one entry leave the UFO

466:     by_block: Dict[str, List[Parameter]] = {}
467:     for p in params:

478:                         "name twice. Give one of them its own block_name (or, for "
479:                         "scalars, its own order_block)"
480:                     )

1068: \section{Phenomenology of the composite bosons in $pp$ and $ep$ collisions}\label{PhenomenologyCompositeFermions}
1069: 
1070: In this section we study the phenomenology of the composite fermions in $pp$ collisions. We first outline its production and decay mode and then calculate its cross section and decay width. This study leads us to the discussion on the search for $\Pi$ that will be discussed in the next section.
1071: 
1072: 
1073: \subsection{Production and decay of composite bosons $\Pi^{0,\pm}$}
1074: 
1075: As already specified in Sec.~\ref{contact}, 
1076: the composite bosons $\Pi$ can be 
1077: \begin{eqnarray}
1078: &&\Pi^+ ~(\bar du,\bar cs, \bar bt),\nonumber\\
1079: &&\Pi^- ~(\bar ud,\bar sc, \bar tb),\nonumber\\
1080: &&\Pi^0_u ~(\bar uu,\bar ss, \bar tt),\nonumber\\ 
1081: &&\Pi^0_d ~(\bar dd,\bar cc, \bar bb),
1082: \label{comSpecB}
1083: \end{eqnarray}
1084: for the charge sector $Q=+,-,0$ 
1085: respectively, and the corresponding composite bosons 
1086: of the higher generation of families in the SM.
1087: 
1088: The kinematics of the processes is derived in the center of mass frame of $pp$ collisions and virtual processes 
1089: of $\Pi$ are not considered. If the energy $\sqrt{s}$ in the parton centre of mass frame is larger than composite boson masses, the following resonant process can occur:
1090: \begin{eqnarray}
1091: pp &\rightarrow&  ~\Pi
1092: \label{ppfFB}
1093: \end{eqnarray}
1094: where the composite bosons $\Pi$ (\ref{comSpecB}) formed by Standard Model fermions 
1095: of the higher generation of families. The kinematics of final states is simple in the centre of mass frame of $pp$ collisions.
1096: 
1097: If we neglect the quark-family mixing, the previous process can manifest at parton level as:
1098: \begin{eqnarray}
1099: u~\bar{d} &\rightarrow& \Pi^+,\label{udB}\\
1100: d~\bar{u} &\rightarrow& \Pi^-,\label{udbarB}\\
1101: u~\bar{u} &\rightarrow&  \Pi^0_u \label{uuB},\\
1102: d~\bar{d} &\rightarrow& \Pi^0_d.\label{ddB}
1103: 
1104: 
1105: \end{eqnarray}
1106: 
1107: The composite boson $\Pi$ can decay through the two different channels: two SM quarks $q q^\prime$, via the contact 
1108: interactions in Eqs.~(\ref{ciqlB}-\ref{iqlBu}), two SM gauge bosons $\tilde G\tilde G'$ 
1109: via the contact interactions in Eqs.~(\ref{cpg}-\ref{cpgg}). 
1110: Then the composite fermion $\Pi$ decays as:
1111: \begin{eqnarray}
1112: \Pi~&\rightarrow& ~ qq^\prime ,\label{FqqB} \\
1113: \Pi~ &\rightarrow& \tilde G\tilde G'.\label{FPB} 
1114: \end{eqnarray}
1115: The full decay chain is:
1116: \begin{eqnarray}
1117: pp &\rightarrow& \Pi  \rightarrow ~ qq^\prime ,\\
1118: pp &\rightarrow& \Pi  \rightarrow ~ \tilde G\tilde G'.
1119: \end{eqnarray}

1121: It appears clear, considering all the possible flavours of $\Pi$ (\ref{comSpecB}), that a large range

1297: We turn to the pair production of composite particles (fermion and boson) by SM gauge bosons, in particularly by gluons. The composite particles are made of SM quarks and leptons. Therefore, they have SM quantum numbers to couple to SM gauge bosons. These couplings in principle are new parameters of the theory. However, If SM gauge bosons, here we particularly mean gluons,  have energies comparable to composite scale, namely the composite particle masses $M_{F,\Pi}\sim {\mathcal O}(TeV)$, then gluons interact with the quark constitute inside the composite particle. In this case, the strength of gluon coupling to composite particle can be approximately represented by QCD strong coupling $g_s=\sqrt{\alpha_s}$. This is the case for the pair productions of composite particle $\Pi, F$ and anti composite particle $\Pi^\dagger, F^\dagger$ by gluon and gluon collisions,
1298: \begin{eqnarray}
1299: g+g~&\rightarrow& ~ \Pi + \Pi^\dagger ~~{\rm or}~~F + F^\dagger,\label{FqqBql} 
1300: \end{eqnarray}
1301: The reason is that in center of mass frame, gluon and gluon collision energy must be larger than the energy threshold 
1302: $2 M_{F,\Pi}$ to produce two composte particles flying apart, back-to-back. The composite particle and anti composite particle have the same mass. Here, we may consider the lepton-quark composite states, since their decay modes (topologies) are distinct from the SM QCD background.  But the discussions are the same for the pair productions of other composite particles in general.
1303: 
1304: This situation is very much like the Breit-Wheeler process of electron-positron pair production by light-light collision $\gamma+\gamma \rightarrow e^++e^-$. Thus, learning from the QED calculation as shown two tree-level Feynman diagrams in Fig.~\ref{ggpair}, we can write the cross-section as 
1305: \begin{eqnarray}
1306: \sigma_{gg\rightarrow FF^\dagger ~{\rm or}~ \Pi\Pi^\dagger}~&\approx& ~ \frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{\alpha_s}{M_{F,\Pi}}\right)^2(1-\hat\beta^2)
1307: \Big[2\hat\beta^2(\hat\beta^2-2)+(3-\hat\beta^4)\ln\Big(\frac{1+\hat\beta^2}{1-\hat\beta^2}\Big)\Big],\quad \hat\beta^2=\frac{|{\bf p}|}{{\mathcal E}_{gg}}\label{ggpaircross} 
1308: \end{eqnarray}
1309: where ${\mathcal E}_{gg}$ is the two gluons colision energy in CM. Here we use approximation $\sigma_{gg\rightarrow FF^\dagger ~{\rm or}~ \Pi\Pi^\dagger}~\approx ...$, because we approximate the coupling between gluon and composite particle to be the QCD coupling $g_s$. For the energy ${\mathcal E}_{gg}\gg M_{F,\Pi}$, the pair-production cross-section yields
1310: \begin{eqnarray}
1311: \sigma_{gg\rightarrow FF^\dagger ~{\rm or}~ \Pi\Pi^\dagger}~&\approx& ~ \pi \left(\frac{\alpha_s}{M_{F,\Pi}}\right)^2\left(\frac{M_{F,\Pi}}{{\mathcal E}_{gg}}\right)^2.
1312: \label{ggpaircrossa} 
1313: \end{eqnarray}
1314: Only the composite particle masses are involved, no other new parameters like $g_{_Y}$. This process should have the biggest cross section (absorption of gluons), if the gluons collision energy is over the energy threshold $M_{F,\Pi}$ of pair production of composite particles. The decay modes of back-to-back composite particles follow discussions before.

1610: decay into two SM gauge bosons $\tilde G\tilde G'$ in Sec.~(\ref{spgg}). We have following three catalogs and we can calculate the branching ratios to see which channel is relevant and experimentally interesting 
1611: 
1612: The processes with photon in final state are
1613: \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
1614: \item Two back-to-back photons (diphoton) for the channel (\ref{cpg}) ${\mathcal B}=\Gamma_{\Pi\rightarrow\gamma\gamma}/\Gamma_{\rm tot}$; 
1615: \item back-to-back photon and a wide jet 
1616: for the channel (\ref{cpgz}) are final states. 
1617: \end{enumerate}
1618: 
1619: The processes with $W^\pm$ or $Z^0$ in final state are, two back-to-back boosted gauge 
1620: bosons  $Z^0$ (\ref{cpzz}) or $W^\pm$ (\ref{cpww})
1621: are high-energetic boosted intermediate
1622: states, most probably leading to: 
1623: \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
1624: \item a back-to-back
1625: wide dijet of four quarks for $W^\pm$ and $Z^0$ hadronic decays; 
1626: \item back-to-back lepton-pair beams of four leptons 
1627: for $W^\pm$ and $Z^0$ leptonic decay;
1628: \item a wide jet 
1629: and a lepton-pair beam in the combination of cases (i) and (ii). 
1630: 
1631: Instead, two back-to-back photons (diphoton) for the channel (\ref{cpg}), and back-to-back photon and a wide jet 
1632: for the channel (\ref{cpgz}) are final states. 
1633: \end{enumerate}
1634: 
1635: The processes (\ref{pgugu}) with  two gluons $\tilde g$ in final state are, 
1636: \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
1637: \item two gluons (\ref{pgugu}) back-to-back jets, does it fuse to a Higgs then decay to two photons in finite state ?;
1638: 
1639: 
1640: \end{enumerate}
1641: Which channel 
1642: is more relevant for detections, depending not only on theoretical 
1643: branching ratios in principle, but also on experimental measurements in practice. 
1644: 
1645: The widths of these 
1646: $\Pi^0$-decay channels are $\Gamma_{\Pi^0\rightarrow \tilde G\tilde G'}$ (\ref{pg}-\ref{ggrate}), and the total 
1647: $\Pi^0$-decay  width is $\Gamma_{\rm tot}$ (\ref{ptotal}). 
1648: The branching ratios are Eqs.~(\ref{pqq}) and (\ref{pgg}).
1649: As a result, in $pp$ collision the cross section of the $\Pi^0$ production 
1650: and decay to two back-to-back standard jets and/or gauge bosons is (\ref{xsecfgg}).
1651: 
1652: The neutral composite boson $\Pi^0$ mass can be inferred by the invariant mass of its resonance location ${\mathcal M}_{\rm all~ channels}=m_{\Pi^0}$. 
1653: The invariant mass ${\mathcal M}_{\gamma\gamma}$ of the diphoton 
1654: channel (\ref{cpg}) gives the constrain $m_{\Pi^{0}}\gtrsim {\mathcal M}_{\gamma\gamma}$. The invariant mass 
1655: ${\mathcal M}_{\Pi^{\pm,0}\rightarrow jj}$ of the dijet even sets the constrain on the composite boson mass $m_{_{\Pi^{\pm,0}}}$.
1656: Due to the smallness of gauge interactions and quark-family mixing (off-diagonal elements of the CMK matrix), the branching ratios of $\Pi^\pm$ decay to other quark families are neglected, and $m_{\Pi^\pm} \approx m_{\Pi^0}$.
1657:  
1658: 
1659: 
1660: \section{Search for $\Pi$ at the LHC}
1661: \label{SearchForBAtTheLHC}
1662: After having discussed the production and decay of $\Pi$ and its cross-section, width, and decay branching ratio, we now examine these results in terms of parameters of the model and derive the possible final states and their topologies, highlighting their impact to the current program of beyond SM searches at the LHC.
1663: 
1664: 
1665: \subsection{Branching ratios and topology of $\Pi$ with respect to model parameters}\label{bran}
1666: In order to present the branching ratios of different possible 
1667: channels in terms of parameters of the model, 
1668: we are bound to discuss physically sensible 
1669: parameters to explore. This model has four parameters that can be rearranged to three dimensionless parameters for a given $\Lambda$ value:
1670: $
1671: (\Lambda, m_F, F_\Pi, m_\Pi) \rightarrow 
1672: ( m_F/\Lambda, F_\Pi/m_\Pi, m_\Pi/m_F).
1673: $
1674: 
1675: The ratio $m_F/\Lambda < 1$ ($m_\Pi/\Lambda < 1$)
1676: of the composite fermion (boson) mass and the basic composite scale 
1677: $\Lambda$ gives us an insight into the dynamics of composite fermion (boson) 
1678: formation. 
1679: In addition, as the parameters $m_\Pi$  and $F_\Pi$ represent the same dynamics of composite boson formation we use the $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ ratio.
1680: Finally, to take into account the feature that a composite fermion $F$ is composed by a composite boson and an elementary SM fermion, we adopt the ratio  $m_\Pi/m_F < 1$ as a parameter.  
1681: As a result, for given $\sqrt{s}$ and $\Lambda$ values, we have three parameters 
1682: $m_F/\Lambda$, $F_\Pi/ m_\Pi$, and $m_\Pi/m_F$ to represent the results of 
1683: the possible branching ratios. 
1684: 
1685: Figure \ref{AllBr} shows three sets of plots for the branching ratios of $F \rightarrow \bar f qq^\prime$ and $F \rightarrow \bar f \Pi$ (left column), $\Pi \rightarrow qq^\prime$ and $\Pi \rightarrow G\tilde G^\prime$ (center column), and the full decay chains 
1686: $F \rightarrow \bar f qq^\prime$, $F \rightarrow \bar f \Pi \rightarrow \bar f qq^\prime$, and $F \rightarrow \bar f \Pi \rightarrow \bar f G\tilde G^\prime$ (right column). These branching ratios are plotted with respect to the $m_\Pi/m_F$ ratio and for the values of $F_\Pi/\,m_\Pi=0.8$, $F_\Pi/\,m_\Pi=5$, $F_\Pi/\,m_\Pi=15$. 
1687: Note that 
1688: the branching ratios of $F \rightarrow f qq^\prime$ and $F \rightarrow f \Pi$ (left column) do not depend on $m_F/\Lambda$, which can be seen from Eqs.~(\ref{decayE0},\ref{fep}) and (\ref{gtfeqq}). For the $\Pi^\pm$ decay, the channel (\ref{Gamma_pqq}) is unique, so the branching ratio is one, independent of $m_F/\Lambda$. Whereas the $\Pi^0_{u,d}$ decays also to $G^\prime G$, see Eqs.~(\ref{pqq}) and (\ref{pgg}), and the branching ratio depends on $m_F/\Lambda$. However, in the regime of $m_\Pi/m_F$ we consider, the branching ratio of $\Pi^0_{u,d}\rightarrow G^\prime G$ is very small and negligible, compared with the branching ratio of $\Pi^0_{u,d}\rightarrow q^\prime q$. Therefore, our results of branching ratio of $F$ decay presented in Fig.~\ref{AllBr} 
1689: are independent of the parameter $m_F/\Lambda$. As a result, regarding the branching ratio and topologies of $F$ decay, the model effectively depends only on two parameters $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ and $m_\Pi/m_F$. However, the cross section of $F$ production depends on the parameter $m_F/\Lambda$, as indicated in Eq. \ref{csE0}.
1690: 
1691: 
1692: 
1693: 
1694: 
1695: 
1696: In Fig.~\ref{AllBr}, 
1697: it is shown that the branching ratios $F\rightarrow f q\bar q ~{\rm direct}$ (\ref{Eeqqdirect}) and $F\rightarrow f\Pi \rightarrow f q\bar q~{\rm indirect}$ (\ref{Eepqq}) 
1698: tend to swap each other for different values of $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$. 
1699: Increasing the coupling $F_\Pi$ (and the ratio $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$) of composite boson $\Pi$ to its two constituents  ($q\bar q$), see 
1700: contact interactions (\ref{ciqlB},\ref{iqlBd},\ref{iqlBu}), 
1701: the branching ratios $F\rightarrow f\Pi \rightarrow f q\bar q~{\rm indirect}$ (\ref{Eepqq}) 
1702: becomes dominant over 
1703: the branching ratios $F\rightarrow f q\bar q ~{\rm direct}$ (\ref{Eeqqdirect}). We thus consider two reference cases of $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$: 
1704: \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
1705: \item $F_\Pi/m_\Pi\lesssim 0.8$ where $F\rightarrow f q\bar q ~{\rm direct}$ dominates. We have verified that for the value 0.8 the direct production dominates by at least a factor 10 over the production with the $\Pi$ for all values of $m_\Pi/m_F$.
1706: \item $F_\Pi/m_\Pi\gtrsim 5$ where $F\rightarrow f\Pi \rightarrow f q\bar q~{\rm indirect}$ (\ref{Eepqq}) becomes relevant for all values of $m_\Pi/m_F$ and dominates above $m_\Pi/m_F>$0.2 over $F\rightarrow f q\bar q ~{\rm direct}$. We notice from Fig.~\ref{AllBr} 
1707: that as $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ increases above 15, the decay $F\rightarrow f\Pi \rightarrow f q\bar q~{\rm indirect}$ dominates over all possible decays for all values of $m_\Pi/m_F$. 
1708: \end{enumerate}
1709: 
1710: The expected topologies related to the phenomenology of $F$ are summarized in Table \ref{FinalStatesTopologiesF0}, considering the two complementary cases of $F_\Pi/m_\Pi\leq 0.8$ and $F_\Pi/m_\Pi\geq 15$. These cases are representative of the topology of $F$ in all the phase space, including the intermediate region $0.8 < F_\Pi/m_\Pi < 15$, in which the decay $F\rightarrow f q\bar q ~{\rm direct}$ or $F\rightarrow f\Pi \rightarrow f q\bar q~{\rm indirect}$ dominates depending on the specific value of $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ considered. To this purpose we provide in Appendix~\ref{Br_Fpimpi_1_15_step1} the total decay branching ratios corresponding to Fig.~\ref{AllBr} (right column) for values of $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ between 1 and 14, increasing in step of 1. We further outline that the value 0.2 for $m_\Pi/m_F$ that separates the boosted from the resolved topology when $F$ decays through a $\Pi$ is indicative and may vary based on the mass of $F$. We have verified, using CalcHEP, that for a mass of $F$ of 1 TeV, the two quarks decaying from the $\Pi$ originating from $F$ are indeed within a $\Delta R(q,\bar{q}')$ below 0.8, which determines the cone size of a large-radius jets suitable for boosted jet at the LHC experiments. For a mass of $F$ of 7 TeV instead, the value 0.2 is lowered to 0.15 to guarantee $\Delta R(q,\bar{q}')<0.8$, as for higher masses of $F$ its width increases.

738: ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];

LGauge := Block[{mu,nu,ii,aa}, 
  ExpandIndices[-1/4 FS[B,mu,nu] FS[B,mu,nu] - 1/4 FS[Wi,mu,nu,ii] FS[Wi,mu,nu,ii] - 1/4 FS[G,mu,nu,aa] FS[G,mu,nu,aa], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];

LFermions := Block[{mu}, 
  ExpandIndices[I*(
    QLbar.Ga[mu].DC[QL, mu] + LLbar.Ga[mu].DC[LL, mu] + uRbar.Ga[mu].DC[uR, mu] + dRbar.Ga[mu].DC[dR, mu] + lRbar.Ga[mu].DC[lR, mu]), 
  FlavorExpand->{SU2W,SU2D}]/.{CKM[a_,b_] Conjugate[CKM[a_,c_]]->IndexDelta[b,c], CKM[b_,a_] Conjugate[CKM[c_,a_]]->IndexDelta[b,c]}];

LHiggs := Block[{ii,mu, feynmangaugerules},
  feynmangaugerules = If[Not[FeynmanGauge], {G0|GP|GPbar ->0}, {}];
 
  ExpandIndices[DC[Phibar[ii],mu] DC[Phi[ii],mu] + muH^2 Phibar[ii] Phi[ii] - lam Phibar[ii] Phi[ii] Phibar[jj] Phi[jj], FlavorExpand->{SU2D,SU2W}]/.feynmangaugerules
 ];

LYukawa := Block[{sp,ii,jj,cc,ff1,ff2,ff3,yuk,feynmangaugerules},
  feynmangaugerules = If[Not[FeynmanGauge], {G0|GP|GPbar ->0}, {}];
 
  yuk = ExpandIndices[
   -yd[ff2, ff3] CKM[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].dR [sp, ff3, cc] Phi[ii] - 
    yl[ff1, ff3] LLbar[sp, ii, ff1].lR [sp, ff3] Phi[ii] - 
    yu[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].uR [sp, ff2, cc] Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj], FlavorExpand -> SU2D];
  yuk = yuk /. { CKM[a_, b_] Conjugate[CKM[a_, c_]] -> IndexDelta[b, c], CKM[b_, a_] Conjugate[CKM[c_, a_]] -> IndexDelta[b, c]};
  yuk+HC[yuk]/.feynmangaugerules
 ];

LGhost := Block[{LGh1,LGhw,LGhs,LGhphi,mu, generators,gh,ghbar,Vectorize,phi1,phi2,togoldstones,doublet,doublet0},
  (* Pure gauge piece *) 	
  LGh1 = -ghBbar.del[DC[ghB,mu],mu];
  LGhw = -ghWibar[ii].del[DC[ghWi[ii],mu],mu];
  LGhs = -ghGbar[ii].del[DC[ghG[ii],mu],mu];

1832: So far we have presented the studies relying on the first SM generation, i.e. considering the electron flavour of $F$ ($F = E$). However, these discussions and calculations are straightforwardly generalized to the second and third SM generations, and in the text we keep the general notation $F$ instead of $E$. At the 
1833: leading order of only contact interactions being taken into account, the formulae of cross-sections, decay rates and 
1834: branching ratios of the second and third generations are the same as those of the first generation, however composite fermions $F$ and their productions, decay channels and rates are different, depending 
1835: on the values of their parameters $m_F$, $m_\Pi$ and $F_\Pi$, which
1836: vary from one SM generation to another.
1837: The reasons are that the effective couplings $\sim g_*^2/\Lambda^2$ and 
1838: $\sim g_{_Y}$ of contact interactions can be different, due to the 
1839: modifications from the flavor mixing and gauge interactions. 
1840: 
1841: However, we neglect these modifications 
1842: in this article, and expect the variations of masses 
1843: $m_F$, $m_\Pi$, decay 
1844: constant $F_\Pi$ to be small. In this sense, there are two basic 
1845: parameters $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ and $m_\Pi/m_F$ 
1846: for each SM generation to be determined by different channels and 
1847: their topologies in LHC experiments discussed in next sections.

1865: We now summarize on the possible signatures with which $F$ can manifest at the LHC. We remark that $F$ can have the different flavours corresponding to the Standard Model flavours of $f$ and the fact that these particles are not necessarily mass degenerate. This implies that they can have different masses with which they can appear within the energy reach of the LHC, and thus they have to be searched for independently. Based on the flavours of $f$, we expect 8 different final states to be investigated for the pair $fF$ produced in the process $pp\rightarrow fF$, which are: $eE,\mu M,\tau\mathcal{T},\nu N,jJ,cC,bB,tT$. Here, we consider one single channel ($\nu N$) for all the $\nu$ neutrinos of the Standard Model and one single channel ($jJ$) for the $u,d,s$ quarks. We notice that the flavour $cC$ is taken separately, because of the improving performances in c-tagging algorithms at the LHC (\cite{cTagATLAS, cTagCMS}) and dedicated searches for new physics with $c$ quarks in the final state (\cite{cTagSearchATLAS, cTagSearchCMS}). Moreover, we distinguish the three topologies (resolved with and without $\Pi$ and boosted) explained in the previous paragraph, so that we have in total 24 different signatures that have to be considered in order to pursue a comprehensive search of $F$. 
1866: 
1867: 
1868: In Table ~\ref{FinalStatesTopologiesF} we outline these signatures based on the flavours $f$ and $F$, the possible topology, the corresponding final states, and the LHC search that, to the best of our knowledge, could be more sensitive to searching for $F$. In the last column, we further report on features of $F$ and its decay that have not been exploited directly in the cited LHC searches and could be used to improve possible future searches dedicated to $F$. We especially remark that the $F$ quark flavours appear to be completely unexplored yet and we urge on the importance of carrying out specific analyses at LHC to investigate it. This is certainly noteworthy and can have a relevant impact on the beyond the SM physics program of the LHC.
1869: 
1870: 
1871: We notice that, despite possible and with a peculiar signature, the channel $f F \rightarrow f (\bar f \Pi) \rightarrow f (\bar f (\tilde G\tilde G^\prime))$ is negligible since the decay $\Pi^0 \rightarrow (\tilde G\tilde G^\prime)$ is only relevant for $F_\Pi/\,m_\Pi=0.1$ when, however, the decay $F \rightarrow f (\Pi)$ has a branching ratio close to zero. Because of this we do not include this case in Table ~\ref{FinalStatesTopologiesF} and we point out that this case would become of interest in the case $F$ is found in one of the possible signatures mentioned above, to study the nature of the new particle. \comment{It should be mentioned that these gauge bosons $\tilde G\tilde G'$ in Eq.~(\ref{PiGG}) can be two gluons that possibly fuse to a Higgs particle in the final states. Do we keep this part? how is it related to BSM searches? should we mention about future studies on this case?} 
1872: 
1873: We put emphasis on the case of the composite fermions 
1874: $F=N^0,\bar N^0, N^+,N^-$ for the final state $\nu\nu qq^\prime$, where $\nu\bar\nu$ stands for the pairs of the SM left-handed neutrino $\nu^e_L$ 
1875: and/or sterile right-handed neutrino $\nu^e_R$, as the latter is a candidate of dark-matter particles. 
1876:

1992: In this section we provide a discussion of the bounds of the model parameters taking as a reference the case $F = E$ and the final state $eeqq^\prime$ that has been shown to be sensitive to a wide portion of the parameter space of the model in the previous section. For this purpose, we
1993: recast the 95\% confidence level (C.L.) experimental upper limit on $\sigma(pp\rightarrow eeqq^\prime)$ using a recent analysis~\cite{LARFP2017} 
1994: of 2.3 fb$^{-1}$ data from the 2015 Run II of the LHC by the CMS collaboration with respect to the predictions of the  model of composite fermions discussed in this article. Note that both electrons and positrons are collected in the final states of $eeqq^\prime$, electrons and positrons are not distinguished  in the data analysis.
1995: For the case $m_F/\Lambda=1$ one obtains that the composite 
1996: fermions of this model are excluded up to masses 
1997: $m^{\rm ex }_F\approx 4.25$ TeV. 
1998: This result is shown in Figure \ref{recast}, together with the exclusion limits 
1999: $m^{\rm ex }_F\approx 3.3, 2.4,1.5$ TeV for $\Lambda$ fixed at 6, 9 and 12 TeV. 
2000: Figure \ref{2dimlimit} shows the exclusion curve, lower (dashed) line, in the 2-dimensional parameter space $(\Lambda,m_F)$ for the model obtained via  the recasting of the analysis~\cite{LARFP2017} 
2001: of 2.3 fb$^{-1}$ data from the 2015 Run II of the LHC by the CMS collaboration. Here the regions of the parameter space below the curves are excluded. 
2002: 
2003: We also performed a study about the potential of a dedicated analysis in the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) conditions (center of mass energy of 14 TeV and luminosity of 3 ab$^{-1}$). We used CalcHEP to generate the processes and DELPHES \cite{Delphes} to simulate the detector effects. In order to separate the signal from the background, we selected events with $pt_{e_1}\geq$ 180 GeV, $pt_{e_2}\geq$ 80 GeV, $pt_{j_1}\geq$ 210 GeV, $m_{ee}\geq$ 300 GeV ($pt$ is the transverse momentum, $e_1$ the leading electron, $e_2$ the subleading electron, $j_1$ the leading jet and $m_{ee}$ the invariant mass of the two electrons). Then we evaluated the reconstruction and selection efficiencies for signal ($\epsilon_s$) and background ($\epsilon_b$) as the ratio of the selected and the total generated events. From these efficiencies, the signal and  background cross sections ($\sigma_s$, $\sigma_b$) and the integrated luminosity ($L$), it is possible to evaluate the expected number of events for the signal ($N_s$) and the SM background ($N_b$) and finally the statistical significance ($S$):
2004: \begin{equation}
2005: N_s=L\sigma_s\epsilon_s, \quad N_b=L\sigma_b\epsilon_b, \quad S=\frac{N_s}{\sqrt{N_b}}\, .
2006: \end{equation}
2007: The $S=5$ contour curve is shown by the upper (solid) line in Figure \ref{2dimlimit}. It can be used to get indications about the potential for discovery or exclusion with the experiments at the HL-LHC, showing that there is a wide region of the model phase space where the existence of the composite fermions can be investigated;
2008: for the case $m_F/\Lambda=1$ we can reach masses up to $\approx 6.2$ TeV.
2009: We notice that, despite having considered the case of $F = E$ in this section, it could be inferred that the cross section for $F$, which should approximately be the same for all its flavours, is sufficient for the $F$ to appear at the LHC with the statistics already collected at the LHC experiments, and that is expected by the HL-LHC. Based on this result, we recommend that the physics program of the LHC consider the new particles foreseen by this model and their signatures in its investigations.

So far we have presented the studies relying on the first SM generation, i.e. considering the electron flavour of $F$ ($F = E$). However, these discussions and calculations are straightforwardly generalized to the second and third SM generations, and in the text we keep the general notation $F$ instead of $E$. At the 
leading order of only contact interactions being taken into account, the formulae of cross-sections, decay rates and 
branching ratios of the second and third generations are the same as those of the first generation, however composite fermions $F$ and their productions, decay channels and rates are different, depending 
on the values of their parameters $m_F$, $m_\Pi$ and $F_\Pi$, which
vary from one SM generation to another.
The reasons are that the effective couplings $\sim g_*^2/\Lambda^2$ and 
$\sim g_{_Y}$ of contact interactions can be different, due to the 
modifications from the flavor mixing and gauge interactions. 

However, we neglect these modifications 
in this article, and expect the variations of masses 
$m_F$, $m_\Pi$, decay 
constant $F_\Pi$ to be small. In this sense, there are two basic 
parameters $F_\Pi/m_\Pi$ and $m_\Pi/m_F$ 
for each SM generation to be determined by different channels and 
their topologies in LHC experiments discussed in next sections.
    

\subsection{Signatures to search for $F$ at the LHC}














We now summarize on the possible signatures with which $F$ can manifest at the LHC. We remark that $F$ can have the different flavours corresponding to the Standard Model flavours of $f$ and the fact that these particles are not necessarily mass degenerate. This implies that they can have different masses with which they can appear within the energy reach of the LHC, and thus they have to be searched for independently. Based on the flavours of $f$, we expect 8 different final states to be investigated for the pair $fF$ produced in the process $pp\rightarrow fF$, which are: $eE,\mu M,\tau\mathcal{T},\nu N,jJ,cC,bB,tT$. Here, we consider one single channel ($\nu N$) for all the $\nu$ neutrinos of the Standard Model and one single channel ($jJ$) for the $u,d,s$ quarks. We notice that the flavour $cC$ is taken separately, because of the improving performances in c-tagging algorithms at the LHC (\cite{cTagATLAS, cTagCMS}) and dedicated searches for new physics with $c$ quarks in the final state (\cite{cTagSearchATLAS, cTagSearchCMS}). Moreover, we distinguish the three topologies (resolved with and without $\Pi$ and boosted) explained in the previous paragraph, so that we have in total 24 different signatures that have to be considered in order to pursue a comprehensive search of $F$. 


In Table ~\ref{FinalStatesTopologiesF} we outline these signatures based on the flavours $f$ and $F$, the possible topology, the corresponding final states, and the LHC search that, to the best of our knowledge, could be more sensitive to searching for $F$. In the last column, we further report on features of $F$ and its decay that have not been exploited directly in the cited LHC searches and could be used to improve possible future searches dedicated to $F$. We especially remark that the $F$ quark flavours appear to be completely unexplored yet and we urge on the importance of carrying out specific analyses at LHC to investigate it. This is certainly noteworthy and can have a relevant impact on the beyond the SM physics program of the LHC.


We notice that, despite possible and with a peculiar signature, the channel $f F \rightarrow f (\bar f \Pi) \rightarrow f (\bar f (\tilde G\tilde G^\prime))$ is negligible since the decay $\Pi^0 \rightarrow (\tilde G\tilde G^\prime)$ is only relevant for $F_\Pi/\,m_\Pi=0.1$ when, however, the decay $F \rightarrow f (\Pi)$ has a branching ratio close to zero. Because of this we do not include this case in Table ~\ref{FinalStatesTopologiesF} and we point out that this case would become of interest in the case $F$ is found in one of the possible signatures mentioned above, to study the nature of the new particle. \comment{It should be mentioned that these gauge bosons $\tilde G\tilde G'$ in Eq.~(\ref{PiGG}) can be two gluons that possibly fuse to a Higgs particle in the final states. Do we keep this part? how is it related to BSM searches? should we mention about future studies on this case?} 

We put emphasis on the case of the composite fermions 
$F=N^0,\bar N^0, N^+,N^-$ for the final state $\nu\nu qq^\prime$, where $\nu\bar\nu$ stands for the pairs of the SM left-handed neutrino $\nu^e_L$ 
and/or sterile right-handed neutrino $\nu^e_R$, as the latter is a candidate of dark-matter particles. 

Finally, we acknowledge that the final state $f \bar f qq^\prime$ is relevant for a wide range of the parameter space of the model and thus will consider it in the next section and, in particular, the case of $f = e$ and $F = E$ to derive limits on the model parameters based on existing LHC results.

In this section we provide a discussion of the bounds of the model parameters taking as a reference the case $F = E$ and the final state $eeqq^\prime$ that has been shown to be sensitive to a wide portion of the parameter space of the model in the previous section. For this purpose, we
recast the 95\% confidence level (C.L.) experimental upper limit on $\sigma(pp\rightarrow eeqq^\prime)$ using a recent analysis~\cite{LARFP2017} 
of 2.3 fb$^{-1}$ data from the 2015 Run II of the LHC by the CMS collaboration with respect to the predictions of the  model of composite fermions discussed in this article. Note that both electrons and positrons are collected in the final states of $eeqq^\prime$, electrons and positrons are not distinguished  in the data analysis.
For the case $m_F/\Lambda=1$ one obtains that the composite 
fermions of this model are excluded up to masses 
$m^{\rm ex }_F\approx 4.25$ TeV. 
This result is shown in Figure \ref{recast}, together with the exclusion limits 
$m^{\rm ex }_F\approx 3.3, 2.4,1.5$ TeV for $\Lambda$ fixed at 6, 9 and 12 TeV. 
Figure \ref{2dimlimit} shows the exclusion curve, lower (dashed) line, in the 2-dimensional parameter space $(\Lambda,m_F)$ for the model obtained via  the recasting of the analysis~\cite{LARFP2017} 
of 2.3 fb$^{-1}$ data from the 2015 Run II of the LHC by the CMS collaboration. Here the regions of the parameter space below the curves are excluded. 

We also performed a study about the potential of a dedicated analysis in the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) conditions (center of mass energy of 14 TeV and luminosity of 3 ab$^{-1}$). We used CalcHEP to generate the processes and DELPHES \cite{Delphes} to simulate the detector effects. In order to separate the signal from the background, we selected events with $pt_{e_1}\geq$ 180 GeV, $pt_{e_2}\geq$ 80 GeV, $pt_{j_1}\geq$ 210 GeV, $m_{ee}\geq$ 300 GeV ($pt$ is the transverse momentum, $e_1$ the leading electron, $e_2$ the subleading electron, $j_1$ the leading jet and $m_{ee}$ the invariant mass of the two electrons). Then we evaluated the reconstruction and selection efficiencies for signal ($\epsilon_s$) and background ($\epsilon_b$) as the ratio of the selected and the total generated events. From these efficiencies, the signal and  background cross sections ($\sigma_s$, $\sigma_b$) and the integrated luminosity ($L$), it is possible to evaluate the expected number of events for the signal ($N_s$) and the SM background ($N_b$) and finally the statistical significance ($S$):
\begin{equation}
N_s=L\sigma_s\epsilon_s, \quad N_b=L\sigma_b\epsilon_b, \quad S=\frac{N_s}{\sqrt{N_b}}\, .
\end{equation}
The $S=5$ contour curve is shown by the upper (solid) line in Figure \ref{2dimlimit}. It can be used to get indications about the potential for discovery or exclusion with the experiments at the HL-LHC, showing that there is a wide region of the model phase space where the existence of the composite fermions can be investigated;
for the case $m_F/\Lambda=1$ we can reach masses up to $\approx 6.2$ TeV.
We notice that, despite having considered the case of $F = E$ in this section, it could be inferred that the cross section for $F$, which should approximately be the same for all its flavours, is sufficient for the $F$ to appear at the LHC with the statistics already collected at the LHC experiments, and that is expected by the HL-LHC. Based on this result, we recommend that the physics program of the LHC consider the new particles foreseen by this model and their signatures in its investigations.

{\bfseries Appendix: Leptoquark four-fermion operators}\label{LQfourfermion}

Based on the dynamics of strong four-fermion couplings (\ref{q1}),  
the composite bosons 
$\Pi^\pm$ and $\Pi^0_{u,d}$ in Table V of Ref.~\cite{Leonardi:2018jzn} are produced in the quark-quark channel, 
\begin{eqnarray}
&&G_{\rm cut}\,\left[(\bar\psi^{bi}_Lu_{Rb})(\bar u^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})+(\bar\psi^{bi}_Ld_{Rb})(\bar d^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})\right] + {\rm h.c.}.\label{qbhlql}
\end{eqnarray}
Whereas LQ particles produce in the leptoquark channels of three types, 
\begin{eqnarray}
&&G_{\rm cut}\, \Big[(\bar\ell^{i}_Le_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})
+(\bar\ell^{i}_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\psi_{Lia})\Big] + {\rm h.c.},
\nonumber\\

&&G_{\rm cut}\, \Big[(\bar\ell^{i}_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\ell_{Li})
+(\bar\ell^{i}_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\ell_{Li})\Big]+ {\rm h.c.},
\nonumber\\
&&G_{\rm cut}\, \Big[(\bar\psi_{Lia}\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}\psi_{Lia})
+(\bar\psi_{Lia}e_{R})(\bar e_{R}\psi_{Lia})\Big] + {\rm h.c.},
\label{bhlql}

\end{eqnarray}
where the elementary fermion fields are the SM doublet $\ell^i_L=(\nu^e_L,e_L)$ and singlet $e_{R}$ with an additional right-handed neutrino $\nu^e_{R}$ for leptons;
$\psi_{Lia}=(u_{La},d_{La})$ and $u^a_{R}, d^a_{R}$ for quarks, 
where the color $a,b$ and $SU_L(2)$-isospin $i$ indexes are summed over. The four-fermion operators are SM gauge-symmetric and fermion-number conserving.
We explicitly give quark-lepton channels,
\begin{eqnarray}
&&G_{\rm cut}\,\Big[(\bar e_Le_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}d_{La})
+(\bar\nu^{e}_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}u_{La})+ (\bar\nu^{e}_Le_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}u_{La})\Big] + {\rm h.c.},
\label{bhlqlex}\\
&&G_{\rm cut}\,\left[(\bar\nu^e_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}\nu^e_{L})+
(\bar e_Lu^a_{R})(\bar u^a_{R}e_{L})
+(\bar\nu^e_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}\nu^e_{L})+
(\bar e_Ld^a_{R})(\bar d^a_{R}e_{L})\right] + {\rm h.c.},\nonumber\\
&&G_{\rm cut}\,\left[(\bar u^a_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}u^a_{L})
+(\bar d^a_L\nu^e_{R})(\bar \nu^e_{R}d^a_{L})+ (\bar u^a_L e_{R})(\bar e_{R}u^a_{L})
+(\bar d^a_L e_{R})(\bar e_{R}d^a_{L})\right] + {\rm h.c.}.\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
Operators (\ref{bhlql}) or (\ref{bhlqlex})
are for the first generation, 
$\nu^e,e,u,d \rightarrow \nu^\mu,\mu,c,s$ for the second generation, and $\nu^e,e,u,d \rightarrow \nu^\tau,\tau,t,b$ for the third generation.

$SU_L(2)\times U_Y(1)$ chiral symmetric group of the $U_Y(1)$-hypercharge $Y=-1/2$ or $Y=1/2$. }

We attempt to study 
the decays of composite bosons. 
For the sake of simplicity, we 
adopt the first quark family $\psi^i_L=(u,d)_L$ and $\psi_R=u_R,d_R$ for illustrations. For the $u$-channel, the massive composite boson 
$\Pi^i=(\bar u_R\psi^i_L)$, which is an $SU_L(2)$ 
doublet and $U_Y(1)$ charged $Y=-1/2$, can expressed in terms of scalar 
and pseudo scalar fields,
\begin{eqnarray}
\Pi^i=(g^*/F_\Pi)^2(\bar u_R\psi^i_L)=(1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\left[(\bar u\psi^i)
-(\bar u\gamma_5\psi^i)\right].

\label{sacomp}
\end{eqnarray}
There are four components    
\begin{eqnarray}
S^0&=&\bar uu,\quad S^{-} =\bar ud\,; \quad 
\quad \Pi^0_u=\bar u\gamma_5u, 
\quad \Pi^-=\bar u\gamma_5d 
\label{4comp}
\end{eqnarray} 
where the isospin index $i=1,2$ are relabeled as $i'=0,\pm$ 
indicating the neutral or charged component. The $S^{}$
For the $d$-channel, by the substitution $u\rightarrow d$ in 
Eqs.~(\ref{sacomp}) and (\ref{4comp}), we have
\begin{eqnarray}
\Pi^i&=&(g^*/F_\Pi)^2(\bar d_R\psi^i_L)=(1/2)(g^*/F_\Pi)^2\left[(\bar d\psi^i)
-(\bar d\gamma_5\psi^i)\right],\nonumber\\

S^0&=&\bar dd,\quad S^+ =\bar du\,; \quad 
\quad \Pi^0_d =\bar d\gamma_5d, 
\quad \Pi^+=\bar d\gamma_5u,
\label{4compd}
\end{eqnarray}
where the factor $(g^*/F_\Pi)^2$ is not explicitly written in the second line of Eqs. (\ref{4comp}) and (\ref{4compd}). 
The neutral state $\Pi^0$ has the contributions from Eqs.~(\ref{4comp}) and (\ref{4compd}) that can be mixed up, but is different from the normal pion $\pi^0=(\bar uu-\bar dd)/\sqrt{2}$ in the $SU(3)$ quark model where the minus sign comes from the isospin $\tau^3=(1,-1)$. 
The discussions can be 
generalised to other families. The second and third 
families of composite bosons are simply replicated by the replacements 
$u\rightarrow c, t$ and $d\rightarrow s, b$. There is no mixing among three
families of composite bosons. 

However, the massive pseudo scalar fields $\Pi^{0,\pm}$ 
(\ref{4comp},\ref{4compd})  and 
the QCD pion fields $\pi^{0,\pm}$ have the same quantum numbers of the SM symmetries. Moreover, we shall show the pseudo-scalar fields $\Pi^{0,\pm}$
decay into SM elementray particles, in particular the $\Pi^{0}$-decay 
into two SM gauge bosons, analogously to the decay $\pi^0\rightarrow \gamma\gamma$.

\red{In Eqs. (\ref{4comp}) and (\ref{4compd}), $S^{0,\pm}$ represent the scalar components and 
$\Pi^{0,\pm}$ represent the pesudo scalar component. In the following, we will in general use the 
notation $\Pi$ to represent the composite boson, and specify its scalar or pseudo scaler components if necessary. Our previous calculations of the $\Pi\rightarrow q\bar q'$ has taken into account both components (\ref{4compd}). The channels of hadronic decay via gluons should be suppressed by the OZI rule, due to the strong coupling $\alpha_s(energy)$ become smaller at high energies. }

In Eqs.~(\ref{4comp}) and (\ref{4compd}), the scalar component of the composite bosons form composite 
quarkonium states $\bar uu$ and $\bar dd$ that carry the same quantum 
numbers of QCD quarknium states, however, have much larger masses 
$\sim M_{\Pi^{0}}$. It is expected that apart from different kinematic 
threshold, these composite quarkonium states 
in principle undergo all decay channels of QCD quarkonium states. However, These scalar component of 
the composite bosons should decay predominately to two quarks as we calculated in the previous article, note that the effective contact interactions are not QCD-like interactions of confinement. The channels of hadronic decay via QCD gluons should be suppressed by the OZI rule, due to the strong coupling $\alpha_s(energy)$ become smaller at high energies.
